planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Nebbiolo buds and ripens very early and late respectively, needing a long, warm growing season and specific site conditions to reliably ripen its notoriously demanding fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Nebbiolo is the noble red grape of Piedmont, Italy, source of the legendary Barolo and Barbaresco wines, prized for pale color that belies powerful, high-tannin, high-acid wines with distinctive aromas of rose, tar, and dried cherry that develop remarkable complexity with age. The grape buds early, exposing it to spring frost risk, yet ripens very late in the season, one of the last major wine grapes harvested each year, and it is notoriously particular about site, generally performing best on specific hillside exposures that concentrate warmth — a real challenge for growers outside its native Piedmont. Train to a permanent trellis, prioritize a warm, well-exposed site, and be prepared for a long hang time before tannins and flavors reach full ripeness.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

common_name: Pinotage Wine Grape (South African Pinot Noir x Cinsaut Cross)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Pinotage is a vigorous, adaptable vine that tolerates warmer climates better than its Pinot Noir parent.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Pinotage was created in South Africa in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsaut (then locally known as Hermitage), combining the two into a distinctive grape now considered South Africa's signature red wine variety, producing deeply colored wines with bold red and dark fruit character often accompanied by a distinctive smoky, earthy, sometimes rubbery note that divides wine drinkers but has become part of the grape's identity. The vine is considerably more vigorous and heat-tolerant than pure Pinot Noir, adapting well to warmer growing regions where its more finicky parent would struggle, and it produces reliably heavy crops if not deliberately restricted. Train to a permanent trellis, thin crop for concentrated flavor if quality wine is the goal, and manage canopy carefully, since overcropped Pinotage can accentuate unwanted rubbery, volatile aromas.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

common_name: Carménère Wine Grape (Chile's Rediscovered Bordeaux Red)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Carménère is a very late-ripening variety needing a long, warm season with a late first frost to fully mature.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Carménère is one of the original six red grapes of Bordeaux, nearly wiped out in France by the phylloxera epidemic of the late 1800s and long presumed extinct until it was recognized, decades later, growing widely in Chile under vines mistakenly identified and sold as Merlot — a discovery that has since made Carménère something of Chile's signature red grape. Wines are deeply colored with distinctive dark fruit and characteristic green, herbal, bell-pepper notes when not fully ripe, softening into riper black fruit and spice character when the grape achieves full physiological ripeness, which requires a long, warm growing season and late harvest. Train to a permanent trellis, prioritize sites with a long frost-free season, and be prepared to leave fruit hanging later than most other red varieties to avoid the unripe vegetal character the grape is prone to.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

common_name: Albariño Wine Grape (Crisp Coastal Spanish White)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Albariño's notably thick skin gives it above-average resistance to the fungal disease pressure common in humid coastal growing regions.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Albariño is the signature white grape of Galicia in northwestern Spain, known there as Albariño and just across the border in Portugal as Alvarinho, producing crisp, aromatic wines with bright citrus and stone fruit character and a distinctive faint salinity often attributed to the vineyards' proximity to the Atlantic coast. The grape's notably thick skin gives it real practical resistance to the rot and fungal pressure common in the humid, maritime climate of its home region, a useful trait that also helps it perform well in other humid growing areas where thinner-skinned white varieties struggle. Train to a permanent trellis, prioritize good airflow through the canopy, and harvest to preserve the variety's signature bright acidity, since Albariño loses its refreshing character if left to hang too long.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Vermentino is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once established, well suited to warm growing regions.

directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun. Vermentino is a Mediterranean white grape most closely associated with Sardinia, Liguria, and Corsica, prized for producing crisp, refreshing wines with bright citrus and herbal notes and a characteristic faint saline minerality, made in a style well suited to warm-climate coastal cuisine. The vine is naturally heat- and drought-tolerant, retaining useful acidity even in hot growing conditions better than many other white varieties, which has made it an increasingly popular choice for warm-climate plantings outside its traditional Mediterranean range. Train to a permanent trellis, manage vigor through canopy work since the variety can be quite vigorous, and pick based on acid retention rather than sugar alone, since Vermentino's appeal rests heavily on preserving its signature freshness.
sources: University of California Davis Viticulture and Enology
